title: Hávamál
source: Gustav Neckel, Edda: Die Lieder des Codex Regius nebst verwandten Denkmälern, 1st edition (Heidelberg: Carl Winter, 1914), Hávamál, stanzas 80–110, pp. 28–33. Text transcribed from Neckel's page images and reproduced in his normalization exactly — þ, ð, æ, œ, the nasal vowel ǫ, ø, acute length-marks, the -z/-az/-oz middle endings, i for j (sitia, miǫk), -om datives, þvíat as one word. Italicized (editorially emended or expanded) letters are set as plain letters; the emendations that change the sense are noted. Neckel's raised commas marking direct speech (st. 98) are kept. In his apparatus, bold sigla are manuscripts (R = Codex Regius) and italic sigla are scholars (Mh = Müllenhoff, R = Rask, D = Dietrich, J = Finnur Jónsson, Hs = Heusler, Gv = Grundtvig, B = Bugge); the notes here follow that distinction. Eddic poems are cited by stanza, so the margin numbers are stanza numbers. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed classical Old Icelandic, c. 1200. Translations made fresh from the original.
about: The second movement of the Hávamál, running from the end of the proverbs to the break Neckel prints at stanza 110. It begins in the gnomic voice of the Gestaþáttr — praise the day at evening, buy a horse lean — and then turns into something stranger. At stanza 84 begins what Karl Müllenhoff named the ‘first Odin example’: a warning against trusting women, a vast catalogue of things that cannot be relied on, and then, at 91, an admission that men's hearts are exactly as false. What follows is the speaker's own humiliation — he waits in a reed-bed for Billing's daughter and is left a dog tied to her bed — and then, from 104, the theft of the mead of poetry from Suttungr and Gunnlǫð, told by the thief, who admits he repaid her badly. The section ends in another voice altogether, accusing Óðinn of breaking an oath sworn on the sacred ring. Everything printed here is a modern editor's normalization of a single manuscript, the Codex Regius (GKS 2365 4to, c. 1270); the verse is ljóðaháttr, and the margin numbers are stanza numbers.

sentences.t:
Þat er þá reynt,
er þú at rúnom spyrr,
inom reginkunnom,
þeim er gørðo ginnregin
ok fáði fimbulþulr:
þá hefir hann batst, ef hann þegir.
sentences.l:
That is then proved,
when you ask after the runes,
the god-descended ones,
those which the mighty powers made
and the great sage stained:
then he does best if he keeps silent.
sentences.i: This is the test of it, when you come asking after the runes — the runes of divine descent, that the mighty powers made and the great sage stained: a man does best then if he holds his tongue.
sentences.n: Three of the poem's grandest words fall inside six lines: reginkunnr 'sprung from the gods', ginnregin 'the mighty powers', fimbulþulr 'the great sage' — a þulr being a reciter of lore, which is the office the whole poem speaks from. fá is the technical verb for colouring carved runes, with pigment or with blood. The last line is a genuine crux: hann has no clear antecedent, and it is usually taken as the questioner, who does best to say nothing about what he has learned. Neckel's apparatus records that Müllenhoff rearranged the order here, moving 80 up behind 77 and taking 76, 77 and 80 together as the close of the first gnomic poem; Neckel notes the proposal without following it.

sentences.t:
At kveldi skal dag leyfa,
kono, er brend er,
mæki, er reyndr er,
mey, er gefin er,
ís, er yfir kømr,
ǫl, er drukkit er.
sentences.l:
At evening one should praise the day,
a wife, when she is burnt,
a blade, when it is tried,
a maiden, when she is given,
ice, when one gets over it,
ale, when it is drunk.
sentences.i: Praise the day at evening; a wife when she is on the pyre; a blade when it has been tested; a girl when she is married; ice when you are across it; ale when it is drunk.
sentences.n: One verb, leyfa 'praise', carries all six objects from the first line — a list governed from a distance, which is this whole section's favourite shape (st. 85–89 take it to an extreme). brend er is meant literally: a wife earns her praise only after her cremation, when no more of her life is left to go wrong. Watch er in this stanza: at the caesura it is the relative particle 'who, which', and at the end of lines 2–4 and 6 it is the verb 'is'.

sentences.t:
Í vindi skal við hǫggva,
veðri á sió róa,
myrkri við man spialla:
mǫrg ero dags augo.
Á skip skal skriðar orka,
en á skiǫld til hlífar,
mæki hǫggs,
en mey til kossa.
sentences.l:
In a wind one should hew wood,
in fair weather row out to sea,
in the dark talk with a girl:
many are the day's eyes.
Of a ship one should get speed,
and of a shield, for cover,
of a sword a stroke,
and of a girl, for kisses.
sentences.i: Cut your timber in a wind, row out in fair weather, talk with a girl in the dark: the day has many eyes. Ask a ship for speed, a shield for cover, a sword for a stroke, a girl for kisses.
sentences.n: mǫrg ero dags augo — 'many are the eyes of day': daylight sees from every side. Note the trap in line 1: við here is not the preposition 'with' but viðr 'wood, timber' in the accusative, so the line is 'hew wood', not 'hew with'. veðri in line 2 is simply 'in weather'; the sense 'in fair weather' comes from what the line is for. Lines 5–8 alternate two constructions that English flattens into one: orka takes a bare genitive of what you get (skriðar 'of speed', hǫggs 'of a stroke'), but til + genitive for what a thing is for (til hlífar 'for cover', til kossa 'for kisses'). man (neuter) is a bondmaid or young woman; it returns at st. 92.

sentences.t:
Við eld skal ǫl drekka,
en á ísi skríða,
magran mar kaupa,
en mæki saurgan,
heima hest feita,
en hund á búi.
sentences.l:
By the fire one should drink ale,
and on the ice glide,
buy a horse lean,
and a sword grimy,
fatten a horse at home,
and a dog on the farm.
sentences.i: Drink your ale by the fire and travel on the ice; buy a horse lean and a sword grimy; fatten your horse at home and your dog at the farm.
sentences.n: Shrewd advice with an edge: a lean horse and a dirty sword cannot be dressed up by a seller — you can see exactly what you are buying. skríða 'creep, glide' is the ordinary verb for going over ice, whether on bone skates (ísleggir) or on skis. Two words here look like ones you have already met and are not: mar is marr 'steed', not marr 'sea', and búi is bú 'farm, household', not the verb búa 'dwell'.

sentences.t:
Meyiar orðom
skyli manngi trúa,
né því er kveðr kona;
þvíat á hverfanda hvéli
vóro þeim hiǫrto skǫpoð,
brigð í brióst um lagið.
sentences.l:
In a maiden's words
should no man trust,
nor in what a woman says;
for on a wheel that turns
were their hearts fashioned,
fickleness laid in the breast.
sentences.i: Let no man trust a girl's words, nor anything a woman says: their hearts were fashioned on a wheel that never stops turning, and inconstancy laid in their breasts.
sentences.n: Müllenhoff proposed that the 'first Odin example' begins here (and the second at 103), and Neckel records the division in his apparatus. It matters for how the next ten stanzas read: they are not free-standing wisdom but the boast of a speaker who is about to be made a fool of by a woman in st. 96–102. á hverfanda hvéli is often taken as a potter's wheel, though the phrase says only 'on a turning wheel'. vóro þeim hiǫrto skǫpoð is a dative of possession — 'hearts were shaped for them' — a construction Old Norse uses where English uses a possessive. The charge is answered from the other side at st. 91, where the same voice lays it on men. manngi 'no one' is maðr with the suffixed negative -gi. Lines 4–6 are the one passage in this whole section that survives outside the Codex Regius: they are quoted in Flateyiarbók and Hauksbók, which drop þvíat and vary the wording slightly.

sentences.t:
Brestanda boga,
brennanda loga,
gínanda úlfi,
galandi kráko,
rýtanda svíni,
rótlausom viði,
vaxanda vági,
vellanda katli,
sentences.l:
A bursting bow,
a burning flame,
a gaping wolf,
a screeching crow,
a grunting swine,
a rootless tree,
a rising wave,
a boiling kettle,
sentences.i: A bow on the point of snapping, a flame burning, a wolf with its jaws open, a crow screeching, a pig grunting, a tree with no roots, a wave rising, a kettle at the boil —
sentences.n: Stanzas 85–89 are a single enormous sentence. Everything in this catalogue is in the dative, hanging unattached until the verb finally arrives in st. 88: trúi engi maðr 'let no man trust'. The 8 / 8 / 4 division of 85–87 is the received editorial numbering rather than anything the poem observes — the ragged line counts are the evidence — but it is the standard way of citing the poem, so it is kept. The list is built almost entirely of present participles (brestanda, brennanda, gínanda, rýtanda, vaxanda, vellanda; galandi and fallandi carry -i rather than the expected dative -anda, as Neckel prints them). Every item is caught mid-motion, and that is the argument: nothing here holds still long enough to be relied on. bresta is 'to burst, snap' — the bow is about to break, not merely creaking.

sentences.t:
fliúganda fleini,
fallandi báro,
ísi einnættom,
ormi hringlegnom,
brúðar beðmálom
eða brotno sverði,
biarnar leiki
eða barni konungs,
sentences.l:
a flying dart,
a falling wave,
one-night-old ice,
a ring-coiled serpent,
a bride's bed-talk
or a broken sword,
a bear's play
or a king's child,
sentences.i: a spear in flight, a wave falling, ice one night old, a snake lying coiled, a bride's talk in bed or a sword with a break in it, a bear at play or a king's child —
sentences.n: Two compounds attested only here: beð-mál 'bed-speech', and hring-leginn 'ring-lain', of a snake lying coiled. A bear at play is still a bear. A king's child is on the list because he will one day be a king, with a king's memory.

sentences.t:
siúkom kálfi,
siálfráða þræli,
vǫlo vilmæli,
val nýfeldom,
sentences.l:
a sick calf,
a self-willed thrall,
a seeress's fair words,
the newly slain,
sentences.i: a sick calf, a thrall who does as he pleases, a seeress's pleasing words, the freshly killed —
sentences.n: Neckel's st. 87 runs to only four lines; the catalogue simply spills across the numbering without regard for it. val nýfeldom is the collective valr, the slain of a battlefield — do not trust a body to be a corpse until it has cooled. vilmæli is speech meant to please, the kind a vǫlva gives a client who is paying her.

sentences.t:
akri ársánom
trúi engi maðr,
né til snemma syni —
veðr ræðr akri,
en vit syni,
hætt er þeira hvárt —,
sentences.l:
a field sown early
let no man trust,
nor too soon a son —
weather rules the field,
and wit the son,
each of the two is chancy —,
sentences.i: and a field sown early let no man trust, nor put his faith in a son too soon — the weather governs the one and his own wits the other, and both are a gamble.
sentences.n: Here at last is the verb the catalogue has been waiting for since st. 85: trúi engi maðr 'let no man trust', which takes the dative — which is why every item in the list has been in the dative. ár-sáinn 'sown early in the year': sow before the frosts are finished and the field may come to nothing. A second thought is then folded in — the son who cannot be counted on until his own sense has shown itself — with the dashes marking the aside, as Neckel punctuates it.

sentences.t:
bróðurbana sínom,
þótt á brauto mœti,
húsi hálfbrunno,
hesti alskiótom —
þá er iór ónýtr,
ef einn fótr brotnar —:
verðit maðr svá tryggr,
at þesso trúi ǫllo!
sentences.l:
his brother's slayer,
though he meet him on the road,
a half-burnt house,
an all-swift horse —
then the steed is useless
if one foot breaks —:
let a man not grow so sure
that he trusts in all this!
sentences.i: — nor the man who killed his brother, though he meets him out on the road; nor a half-burnt house, nor a horse of great speed: a steed is worth nothing at all if one leg goes. Let no man grow sure enough to trust all of it.
sentences.n: The sentence that began at st. 85 finally closes. verðit is the negated form, verða 'become' with the suffixed -t, 'let (a man) not become'; the Codex Regius was written verðr and corrected to verðit, and without the -t the line says the opposite of what it means. The same manuscript corrects alskiótan to alskiótom in line 4 — Neckel cross-references it to the parallel case at 94, 4. The half-burnt house is the sharpest thing in the list: it is still standing, and it will not stand. Note the poem's care in the first line — it does not claim the brother's killer will strike again, only that meeting him peaceably on the road proves nothing.

sentences.t:
Svá er friðr kvenna,
þeira er flátt hyggia,
sem aki ió óbryddom
á ísi hálom,
teitom, tvévetrom,
ok sé tamr illa,
eða í byr óðom
beiti stiórnlauso,
eða skyli haltr henda
hrein í þáfialli.
sentences.l:
So is the love of women,
of those who think falsely,
as if one drove an unspiked horse
on slippery ice,
a frisky one, two winters old,
and be badly broken in,
or in a raging wind
a rudderless boat,
or a lame man should catch
a reindeer on a thawing fell.
sentences.i: Such is women's love — the love of creatures who think falsely — like driving an unspiked horse over slippery ice, a frisky two-year-old and badly broken in; or handling a rudderless boat in a howling gale; or a lame man trying to run down a reindeer on a thawing mountainside.
sentences.n: Ten lines, well past the usual six of ljóðaháttr: the stanza swells because the images keep coming. óbryddr means 'not calked' — winter shoes were fitted with spikes, and without them a horse on ice has no purchase at all. In line 6 the sentence loses its grip on its own grammar: after four datives (óbryddom, hálom, teitom, tvévetrom) tamr is a nominative, an anacoluthon editors have long noticed. beiti in line 8 is taken as a poetic word for a ship, on the authority of the medieval name-lists, with the verb carried over from aki in line 3 — but aka 'drive' of a boat is odd, and the line is not certain. þá-fiall is a fell in the thaw, wet snow over mud, the worst footing there is, and the hreinn, the reindeer, is the surest-footed animal in the north.

sentences.t:
Bert ek nú mæli,
þvíat ek bæði veit:
brigðr er karla hugr konom;
þá vér fegrst mælom,
er vér flást hyggiom:
þat tælir horska hugi.
sentences.i: Now I speak plainly, for I know both sides of it: a man's heart is false to a woman. We speak most sweetly when we mean it least — and that is what takes in even a clever mind.
sentences.n: The hinge of the whole section. After seven stanzas warning against women, the voice turns and lays the same charge on men — brigðr, the adjective answering the noun brigð that was laid in women's breasts at st. 84. Whether 84–90 and 91–95 were ever composed as one poem is doubted; as Neckel prints them, this is where a boast becomes a confession, and the story of the speaker's own humiliation follows at once. fegrst and flást are superlative adverbs, 'most fairly' and 'most falsely', set against each other across the caesura.

sentences.t:
Fagrt skal mæla
ok fé bióða,
sá er vill flióðs ást fá,
líki leyfa
ins liósa mans:
sá fær, er friár.
sentences.l:
Fairly one must speak
and offer wealth,
he who wishes to win a woman's love,
praise the body
of the bright girl:
he gets, who courts.
sentences.i: Speak fair and offer money, if you want to win a woman's love; praise the bright girl's body. The one who courts is the one who gets.
sentences.n: leyfa 'praise' comes back from st. 81, but as a tactic now rather than a verdict — and fé is money and livestock, so the advice is frankly to pay. man is the bondmaid of st. 82, not a generic girl, which gives líki leyfa its blunt sense: praise her body. sá fær, er friár is a proverb held together by sound, fær against friár, and it stands like a heading over what follows: in st. 96–102 the speaker does precisely this, and it fails completely.

sentences.t:
Ástar firna
skyli engi maðr
annan aldregi:
opt fá á horskan,
er á heimskan ne fá,
lostfagrir litir.
sentences.l:
For love
should no man
ever blame another:
often they take hold of the wise
which get no hold on the fool,
looks fair with desire.
sentences.i: No man should ever blame another for being in love: beauty that stirs desire often catches the wise man where it leaves the fool untouched.
sentences.n: firna takes the accusative of the person and the genitive of the thing blamed, so ástar firna is 'find fault with (someone) for love'. fá á e-n is 'to get a hold on someone'. The subject is held back to the very last word: lostfagrir litir, literally 'desire-fair hues' — the look of someone who makes you want them, which English has no single word for. Neckel queries in his notes whether the fá of line 5 carries the suffixed negative -a; we follow his printed ne fá.

sentences.t:
Eyvitar firna
er maðr annan skal,
þess er um margan gengr guma:
heimska ór horskom
gørir hǫlða sono
sá inn mátki munr.
sentences.l:
In nothing at all
shall a man blame another
for that which comes over many a man:
foolish out of wise
it makes the sons of men,
that mighty desire.
sentences.i: A man should blame no one at all for what comes over so many: that mighty longing turns wise men into fools.
sentences.n: eyvitar is a genitive used as an adverb, 'not a whit'. Line 2 is a crux: the er sits awkwardly, Rask deleted it and Dietrich read ei instead; we translate Neckel's printed text, taking er as the empty particle, and it has no separate counterpart in the English. The subject is withheld to the last line again, exactly as in st. 93 — sá inn mátki munr, 'that mighty desire' — and munr, which spans 'mind, longing, delight', is the word this whole section turns on. Neckel prints the -om of horskom in italic: the Codex Regius reads horskan and the correction is Rask's. hǫlða sono 'the sons of men' is a formula for people in general.

sentences.t:
Hugr einn þat veit,
er býr hiarta nær,
einn er hann sér um sefa:
øng er sótt verri
hveim snotrom manni
en sér øngo at una.
sentences.l:
The mind alone knows
what has its dwelling by the heart,
alone he is with his own soul:
no sickness is worse
for any wise man
than to take joy in nothing.
sentences.i: Only the mind knows what lies close beside the heart; a man is alone with his own thoughts. And for a wise man there is no sickness worse than to find pleasure in nothing at all.
sentences.n: The boasting drops away and what is left is a man alone with himself — and the very next stanza begins the story of how he was made a fool of. Do not let hugr and hiarta collapse into one word: the mind knows what lives beside the heart. una takes the dative of what one is content with, so sér øngo at una is 'to be content with nothing for oneself'. øngo is the dative of engi 'none', which Neckel spells with ø. The Codex Regius reads manni in line 5; hal is Rask's conjecture, which Neckel records but does not adopt.

sentences.t:
Þat ek þá reynda,
er ek í reyri sat
ok vættak míns munar;
hold ok hiarta
var mér in horska mær —
þeygi ek hana at heldr hefik.
sentences.l:
That I found out then,
when I sat in the reeds
and waited for my delight;
flesh and heart
was to me the wise maiden —
yet I have her not any the more.
sentences.i: I learned that by trying it, sitting in the reed-bed waiting for my heart's desire: flesh and heart she was to me, that clever girl — and for all of it, I do not have her.
sentences.n: The first of the two Odin stories begins, and it begins with the verb the poem keeps using for knowledge bought dearly: reyna 'to learn by trying', the same word as st. 80's Þat er þá reynt and st. 102's þá ek þat reynda. Two verbs here carry an enclitic pronoun fused onto the end — vættak is vætta ek 'I awaited', hefik is hefi ek 'I have' — a compression Old Norse verse likes and English cannot reproduce. hold ok hiarta is a nominative predicate: she *was* flesh and heart to him, everything bodily and everything felt. The sting is the last three words, at heldr 'any the more'.

sentences.t:
Billings mey
ek fann beðiom á,
sólhvíta, sofa:
iarls ynði
þótti mér ekki vera,
nema við þat lík at lifa.
sentences.l:
Billing's maiden
I found on the bed,
sun-white, asleep:
an earl's delight
seemed to me to be nothing,
unless to live with that body.
sentences.i: I found Billing's daughter asleep on her bed, sun-white; and an earl's whole happiness seemed to me worth nothing, if I could not live with that body.
sentences.n: Billingr is otherwise unknown — Snorri never tells this story, and the name turns up in the dwarf-list of the Vǫluspá, which may or may not be the same figure. sólhvítr 'sun-white' is barely attested outside this line: skin so pale it looks lit. lík is simply 'body' here (the word later narrows to 'corpse'), and the stanza's frankness is the point.

sentences.t:
‘Auk nær apni
skaltu, Óðinn, koma,
ef þú vilt þér mæla man;
allt ero óskǫp,
nema einir viti
slíkan lǫst saman.’
sentences.l:
‘And towards evening
you shall come, Óðinn,
if you would bespeak a girl for yourself;
all is ruin,
unless two alone know
of such a fault together.’
sentences.i: ‘Come back towards evening, Óðinn, if you want to speak for a girl of your own. It is all ruin unless the two alone know about a shame like this.’
sentences.n: Her answer, which Neckel marks with raised commas as direct speech. She names him — the first time in the whole poem the speaker is identified, and it is a woman saying Óðinn's name to put him off. mæla þér man is 'to bespeak a girl for yourself': the dative þér is a dative of interest pointing back at Óðinn, so the arrangement is for him, not for her. Neckel's apparatus records that the man of line 3 was corrected from mey in the Codex Regius. óskǫp is literally 'un-shapings', the opposite of what is fated or fitting: a monstrous thing. Line 5 has no expressed subject — viti is a plain 3rd plural, 'unless (people) alone know' — and the first-person reading that most translations give follows Finnur Jónsson's emendation ein vitim; we keep Neckel's text. Note what she actually objects to: not the act, but anyone else knowing of it.

sentences.t:
Aptr ek hvarf,
ok una þóttomz,
vísom vilia frá;
hitt ek hugða,
at ek hafa mynda
geð hennar allt ok gaman.
sentences.l:
Back I turned,
and thought myself content,
away from a sure pleasure;
this I thought,
that I would have
all her heart and her delight.
sentences.i: I turned back, thinking myself well pleased to leave a sure pleasure behind; I thought I would have all her heart and all her joy.
sentences.n: Neckel prints una with the n in italic — an editor's correction; the Codex Regius reads unna. þóttomz is the middle voice (later þóttumk), 'it seemed to myself'. The irony is laid on thick: he congratulates himself on giving up a certain thing for a better one. vísom vilia frá is 'away from a sure pleasure' — a sure thing, given up.

sentences.t:
Svá kom ek næst,
at in nýta var
vígdrótt ǫll um vakin:
með brennandom liósom
ok bornom viði,
svá var mér vilstígr of vitaðr.
sentences.l:
So I came the next time,
that the doughty
war-band was all roused:
with burning lights
and with borne wood,
so was a desire-path marked out for me.
sentences.i: So I came the next time — and the whole able war-band was roused, lights burning and torches carried. So a path of desire, or of woe, was appointed for me.
sentences.n: vilstígr is a crux, and the reading decides the tone: with vil- it is 'the path of desire', with víl- 'a path of woe'. Neckel prints vilstígr and notes that Grundtvig read vílstígr and that all the newer editors follow him. The compound is kept visible in the literal layer and both senses in the idiomatic one, because the poem may well intend the collision. of vitaðr is an agentless passive — the path was appointed, not marked out by anyone named. um vakin is the participle of the causative vekia: the war-band was *roused*, which sets up um sofin 'gone to sleep' in the next stanza. bornom viði is 'borne wood' — torches. The joke is that the household turned out in force to light his way, and being lit is exactly what defeats him.

sentences.t:
Auk nær morni,
er ek var enn um kominn,
þá var saldrótt um sofin:
grey eitt ek þá fann
innar góðo kono
bundit beðiom á.
sentences.l:
And towards morning,
when I had come again,
then the hall-troop was asleep:
a dog alone I then found
of the good woman
bound on the bed.
sentences.i: And towards morning, when I came back again, the household were all asleep — and all I found of the good woman was a dog tied to her bed.
sentences.n: The punchline, delivered flat. grey (neuter) is a dog, a cur or lapdog, used contemptuously; many readers take the substitution to be pointedly a bitch, but the word itself carries no sex. innar góðo kono is genitive, 'belonging to the good woman' — the epithet is not withdrawn, which makes it worse. Neckel's apparatus records that the Codex Regius begins the stanza Ok where he prints Auk (compare st. 98), and that Hildebrand put the caesura after eitt.

sentences.t:
Mǫrg er góð mær,
ef gǫrva kannar,
hugbrigð við hali:
þá ek þat reynda,
er it ráðspaka
teygða ek á flærðir flióð;
háðungar hverrar
leitaði mér it horska man,
ok hafða ek þess vetki vífs.
sentences.l:
Many a good maiden is,
if one looks closely,
fickle of heart towards men:
that I found out then,
when the counsel-wise
woman I drew into deceits;
of every humiliation
the clever girl sought for me,
and I had nothing at all of that woman.
sentences.i: Many a good girl, if you look closely, is fickle-hearted towards men. I learned that when I drew the shrewd woman on into deceits: every humiliation there is the clever girl found for me, and of that woman I had nothing whatever.
sentences.n: The moral he draws — and note that he draws it against her. He drew her on (teygia 'to entice, lead on'), she out-thought him, and the stanza still concludes that women are hugbrigð 'fickle of mind'. Every epithet he gives her, here and in the stanzas around, praises her intelligence: ráðspǫk 'wise in counsel' and horsk 'clever' in this stanza, góð in st. 101, horsk again back in st. 96. Neckel prints the final i of vetki in italic as an editor's correction; the Codex Regius reads vetkis. Nine lines.

sentences.t:
Heima glaðr gumi
ok við gesti reifr,
sviðr skal um sik vera,
minnigr ok málugr,
ef hann vill margfróðr vera,
opt skal góðs geta;
fimbulfambi
heitir, sá er fátt kann segia:
þat er ósnotrs aðal.
sentences.l:
A man glad at home
and cheerful towards guests,
prudent about himself he shall be,
of good memory and ready of speech,
if he wants to be much-knowing,
often shall he speak of good;
a mighty booby
he is called, who knows little to say:
that is the nature of the unwise.
sentences.i: A man should be cheerful at home and welcoming to his guests, and shrewd about himself; a good memory and a ready tongue, if he wants to know much; and let him often speak of what is good. The man with little to say is called a mighty booby — that is what the unwise are like.
sentences.n: This is where Müllenhoff put the start of the 'second Odin example', though the stanza itself is plain gnomic wisdom of the Gestaþáttr kind: the seam between the two stories shows. góðs geta is 'to speak of what is good' — geta with the genitive means 'mention', not 'get'. fimbulfambi 'the mighty fool' is one of the poem's best insults and is attested nowhere else — and fimbul- is the same intensifier as in fimbulþulr, the 'mighty sage' of st. 80. The great sage and the great booby are defined by the same thing, whether they can speak; but where st. 80 said a man does best to hold his tongue, this one makes silence the mark of a fool. The poem contradicts itself openly, and the next stanza takes the side of speech. Nine lines.

sentences.t:
Inn aldna iǫtun ek sótta:
nú em ek aptr um kominn;
fátt gat ek þegiandi þar:
mǫrgom orðom
mælta ek í minn frama
í Suttungs sǫlom.
sentences.l:
The old giant I sought out:
now I am come back again;
little I got there by keeping silent:
with many words
I spoke to my own advantage
in Suttungr's halls.
sentences.i: I went to the old giant; now I am back. I got little there by holding my tongue — I talked my way forward, with a great many words, in Suttungr's halls.
sentences.n: The second story, and the method reverses. Everything the poem has praised so far is silence — st. 80's 'he does best if he holds his tongue', the wary guest of the Gestaþáttr — and here Óðinn says flatly that silence got him nothing. mælta ek í minn frama is 'I spoke to my own advantage'; the poem does not use the word for lying, though what follows is a theft by deception. Neckel's apparatus records that the ek of line 1 was added in the margin of the Codex Regius, and that Heusler proposed reading Sóttak inn aldna iǫtun instead.

sentences.t:
Gunnlǫð mér um gaf
gullnom stóli á
drykk ins dýra miaðar;
ill iðgiǫld
lét ek hana eptir hafa
síns ins heila hugar,
síns ins svára sefa.
sentences.l:
Gunnlǫð gave me
on a golden seat
a drink of the precious mead;
an ill repayment
I let her have afterwards
for her whole heart,
for her heavy spirit.
sentences.i: Gunnlǫð gave me, on a golden seat, a drink of the precious mead. I left her an ill return for her whole heart, for her grieving spirit.
sentences.n: The one stanza in the episode that admits what it cost her, and it does not soften the admission: ill iðgiǫld 'evil repayment' is the poem's own verdict on its speaker. The two genitives síns ins heila hugar and síns ins svára sefa are what the repayment is measured against — she gave a whole heart and got that. Whether svárr here is 'heavy with grief' or 'earnest, weighty' is arguable; either way she is the injured party. Seven lines.

sentences.t:
Rata munn
létomk rúms um fá
ok um griót gnaga;
yfir ok undir
stóðomk iǫtna vegir:
svá hætta ek hǫfði til.
sentences.l:
Rati's mouth
I made get me room
and gnaw through the rock;
above and below
stood about me the giants' ways:
so did I risk my head.
sentences.i: I made Rati's mouth eat me out a passage and gnaw through the stone; the roads of the giants ran above me and below. That is how I staked my head.
sentences.n: The grammar carries the point: munn is accusative, so Rati's mouth is not the actor — this is láta with an accusative and an infinitive, 'I made Rati's mouth get room and gnaw'. Óðinn is the one boring in. Rati is the auger that made the tunnel into the mountain, and it is one of the few *named* details this account shares with Snorri's telling in the Skáldskaparmál, which very likely drew on this poem. létomk and stóðomk carry the -mk middle ending, 'for myself' and 'about me'. hætta hǫfði til is 'to risk one's head on it' — the same image as the head-wagers of the wisdom contests, though the fixed formula there is veðia hǫfði.

sentences.t:
Vel keypts litar
hefi ek vel notit,
fás er fróðom vant;
þvíat Óðrerir
er nú upp kominn
á alda vés iarðar.
sentences.l:
Of the well-bought shape
I have made good use,
little is wanting to the wise;
for Óðrerir
is now come up
to the earth's sanctuary of men.
sentences.i: The shape I bought so well has served me well — little is wanting to a wise man. Óðrerir has come up now, into the earth's holy place of men.
sentences.n: Almost nothing in this stanza is secure. litr 'hue, shape' is usually taken as the shape-changing — Óðinn got in as a snake — and vel keypts 'well bought' is then a bitter joke two stanzas after ill iðgiǫld; but Neckel's apparatus records rival readings for the word itself (Vélkeypts from the Corpus Poeticum Boreale, líðar 'of the drink' from Hildebrand, hlutar from Finnur Jónsson), and líðar would give a wholly different sense. The last line is worse: as Neckel prints it, á governs three genitives in a row and no accusative or dative, which is why five editors — Bugge, Grundtvig, Hildebrand, Finnur Jónsson and Gering — each redistribute the same handful of words differently. The rendering here is a construal of an unconstruable line, offered because something has to stand there. Óðrerir is the mead, or the vessel that holds it — the sources disagree — and the name means something like 'stirrer of the spirit'.

sentences.t:
Ifi er mér á,
at ek væra enn kominn
iǫtna gǫrðom ór,
ef ek Gunnlaðar ne nytak,
innar góðo kono,
þeirar er lǫgðomk arm yfir.
sentences.l:
Doubt is upon me
that I would ever have come
out of the giants' courts,
if I had not had Gunnlǫð,
the good woman,
who laid her arm over me.
sentences.i: I doubt I would ever have got out of the giants' courts if I had not had Gunnlǫð, that good woman, who laid her arm across me.
sentences.n: An admission — and the second time in eight stanzas that a woman he has wronged is called in góða kona. lǫgðomk is the -mk middle again, 'laid over me'. ne is the older negative particle (as at st. 93), and nytak is nióta 'to have the use of' in the preterite subjunctive with the enclitic -k 'I': the whole sentence is a past counterfactual. enn is 'ever, still', not 'back'. This is as close as the poem comes to gratitude, and two stanzas later the affair is called an oath-breaking.

sentences.t:
Ins hindra dags
gengo hrímþursar
Háva ráðs at fregna
Háva hǫllo í:
at Bǫlverki þeir spurðo,
ef hann væri með bǫndom kominn
eða hefði hánom Suttungr of sóit.
sentences.l:
On the next day
the frost-giants went
to ask the High One for counsel
in the High One's hall:
after Bǫlverkr they asked,
whether he had come among the gods
or whether Suttungr had made away with him.
sentences.i: Next day the frost-giants went to ask the High One for counsel, in the High One's hall: they asked after Bǫlverkr — whether he had got back among the gods, or whether Suttungr had destroyed him.
sentences.n: The joke is structural. The frost-giants come to Hávi, the High One, to ask what became of Bǫlverkr — and Bǫlverkr, 'Evil-worker', is the name Óðinn used for the theft. They are asking the thief where the thief went. The weak forms of Hávi are identical in the genitive and accusative, so Háva ráðs at fregna is either 'to ask the High One for counsel' (fregna takes the person in the accusative and the matter in the genitive) or 'to ask after the High One's counsel'; we take the first. bǫnd, literally 'the bonds', is a poetic word for the gods; sóa is 'to sacrifice, to make away with'. In the Codex Regius the last word stands as sóitt, itself corrected from sótt; Neckel prints sóit, and does not say whose hand made the correction. Háva in two successive lines is the poem's own title: Hávamál, 'the sayings of the High One'. Seven lines.

sentences.t:
Baugeið Óðinn
hygg ek at unnit hafi:
hvat skal hans tryggðom trúa?
Suttung svikinn
hann lét sumbli frá
ok grœtta Gunnlǫðo.
sentences.l:
A ring-oath Óðinn,
I think, has sworn:
how shall his pledges be trusted?
Suttungr cheated
he let go from the ale-feast
and Gunnlǫð in tears.
sentences.i: Óðinn, I think, has sworn an oath on the ring — how is anyone to trust his pledges? He left Suttungr cheated of the drink, and Gunnlǫð weeping.
sentences.n: The last stanza before the break Neckel prints, and the voice changes: someone else is speaking now, and it is an accusation. A baugeiðr was sworn on the sacred arm-ring kept on the altar, the most binding oath there was, and the stanza says the god who swore it broke it. The poem does not answer the charge — it lets it stand and turns to the Loddfáfnir counsels. Both objects in the last two lines are past participles agreeing with their nouns, Suttung svikinn 'Suttungr cheated' and Gunnlǫðo grœtta 'Gunnlǫð made to weep', setting the two of them side by side as the two things he did.
